name: Proto-Sinaitic alphabetic writing at Serabit el-Khadim
description: Inscriptions from Serabit el-Khadim use an early consonantal alphabet to write a Semitic language. They include alphabetic dedications on a sandstone sphinx that also bears an Egyptian hieroglyphic inscription.

places.note: Temple and mine inscriptions at Serabit el-Khadim in the Sinai Peninsula

date.label: c. 1850–1800 BCE (estimated local use)
date.basis: Parker’s approximate range for local Proto-Sinaitic use rests on dated Egyptian associations and stylistic assessment. The British Museum dates the sphinx to about 1800 BCE.

events.statement: The sandstone sphinx Sinai 345 (British Museum EA41748) has a hieroglyphic inscription naming Hathor and inscriptions in an early Semitic alphabet. Scholars read a dedication to Baʿalat, ‘the Lady’, in the alphabetic text.
events.place_note: Hathor temple at Serabit el-Khadim in southern Sinai
events.caveats: The readings of some signs and the precise chronology remain disputed. The find documents local use of the script.

evidence.supports: Identifies sandstone sphinx, findspot, the two scripts and approximate date.
Analyzes both scripts on Sinai 345 and preserves the stable reading of the dedication while proposing a new reading of the surrounding text.
Uses Egyptian comparanda and archaeological context to assess the date of the sphinx and related local inscriptions.

earliest_record.rationale: A named surviving witness to this local writing practice. The date is approximate and dates a witness of use.

links.statement: The early alphabet attested at Serabit adapted selected Egyptian sign forms to represent consonants in a Semitic language. Palaeographic comparisons identify the Egyptian eye sign as a model for the consonant ʿayin, from the Semitic word for ‘eye’.
links.scope: Adaptation of selected sign forms in the early alphabet. The comparison concerns the Egyptian sign repertoire and has no identified individual exemplar.
links.timing: The local witness is Middle Bronze Age. The place and date of the first adaptation are unresolved.

evidence.supports: Compares Egyptian eye D4 with Serabit examples of ʿayin and describes the reuse of shapes with new consonantal values. Some specific variant prototypes are uncertain.
Reads the consonantal dedication invoking Baʿalat on the sphinx alongside the Egyptian inscription invoking Hathor.
Independently excavated, later sherd supplies a separate early alphabetic example of the eye-shaped consonant ʿayin linked to Egyptian D4 by the authors.

unresolved.note: Which, if any, of the Serabit and Wadi el-Hol inscriptions came first? Chronology, local adaptation and the place of origin require distinct evidence.
Which users adapted the Egyptian signs, which regional script forms did they encounter, and how did this practice move between communities? Evidence of a shared sign form leaves those steps open.
